mainTopic: When to sound the alarm over drought, famine and other disasters, and the meaning of rain since the חורבן
overview: This amud first finishes defining בצורת and כפנא. One test is how far food must travel; רבי חנינא adds a test of price and whether food can be found at all. רבי יוחנן adds that when people have no money, even cheap food means famine, and he remembers seeing this in טבריה. The גמרא then explains how rain can help plants but not trees, trees but not plants, or both but not the בורות. It ends that section with a single downpour, which fills the pits but helps nothing that grows. Two ברייתות then set the rules for sounding the alarm: deadlines of פסח and סוכות, cases of disease and locusts, and what happens in שביעית. Next, רבי אלעזר בן פרטא teaches that rain has been meager since the חורבן, and he explains different kinds of rainy years with parables. Last, the story of נקדימון בן גוריון begins: he borrows water for the pilgrims, and the officer mocks him as the deadline runs out. The story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the definition: drought versus famine by distance
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a definition: a nearby shortage is בצורת, but food that must come from another province is כפנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: …this is a drought. If food has to be brought from one province to another province, that is a famine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a definition that began just before this section. A smaller shortage is called בצורת, and needing food from another province is called כפנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test here is how far food has to travel. When food has to come from a whole other province, the shortage is wider and more serious, so it gets the stronger name כפנא.

keyTerms.meaning: Drought; a shortage of food, but not the worst kind

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two words. בצורת is the milder shortage, and כפנא is the more serious famine.

phrases.english: this is a drought.
Province to province: famine.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְדִינְתָּא אַמְּדִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a definition that started earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Needing to bring food from another province counts as כפנא.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: drought versus famine by price and availability
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא gives a second test. Grain that is pricey but can be found is בצורת. Grain that cannot be found is כפנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: if a סאה of grain costs a סלע but you can find it, that is a drought. If four סאין cost a סלע but you cannot find it, that is a famine.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא gives another way to tell בצורת from כפנא, based on price and whether food can be found at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The main question is whether food is available. If grain is expensive but you can still buy it, that is only בצורת. If it cannot be found at all, even at a lower price, that is כפנא.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure of volume for grain

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chanina said:
A se'a for a sela, and it is available: drought.
Four se'a for a sela, and it is not available: famine.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second test for the same two terms.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food that is expensive but available is בצורת. Food that is unavailable is כפנא.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: when money is scarce, they cry out immediately
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן limits the price test to times when people have money. If money is scarce, even cheap food counts as a crisis right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: they only taught this when money is cheap and food is expensive. But when money is expensive and food is cheap, they cry out about it right away.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן says the price rule only works when people have plenty of money. When nobody has money, they cry out right away, even if food is cheap.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Price alone does not tell you whether people are hungry. If people have no money, cheap food does not help them, so it is treated as a famine and they cry out immediately.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in a certain case (a limiting phrase)
Money is cheap, meaning people have plenty of it
They cry out (with prayer and shofar blasts)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the real question is whether people can actually eat, not just what food costs.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
They only taught this at a time
when money is cheap and produce is expensive,
phrases.notes: "Money is cheap" means everyone has plenty of it.

phrases.english: but when money is expensive and produce is cheap,
they cry out about it immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי חנינא's price-based definition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When money is scarce and food is cheap, they cry out right away.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's memory of hunger in טבריה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן backs up his rule with a memory: food in טבריה was very cheap, yet many people were swollen from hunger because they had no money.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוחנן said: I remember when four סאין cost a סלע, and yet many people in טבריה were swollen from hunger, because they did not have even an איסר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן proves his point with something he saw himself in טבריה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food was cheap, four סאין for a סלע, yet people were starving. That shows cheap food is not enough when people have no coins, which supports his ruling to cry out right away.
steps.whatToRemember: Hunger depends on whether people can buy food, not just on what food costs.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yochanan said:
I remember when there stood (were sold)
four se'a for a sela,
and there were many swollen from famine in Tiberias
because there was not an issar.
phrases.notes: They didn't have even this tiny coin to buy food.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: נְהִירְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: Scarce money with cheap food is a real famine.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's own memory of טבריה.

steps.title: How rain can help plants but not trees, or trees but not plants
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and explains it: gentle rain helps plants, and heavy rain helps trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: rain fell enough for plants but not for trees. That makes sense: plants but not trees happens when gentle rain came but heavy rain did not. Trees but not plants happens when heavy rain came but gentle rain did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה and shows how each of its first two cases can really happen. Starting with בשלמא ("it makes sense") sets up a harder question that comes soon.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plants need soft rain that soaks the surface. Trees need heavy rain that reaches deep roots. So if only one kind of rain falls, only one kind of growth is helped.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (sets up a contrast with a harder case)

phrases.english: They fell for the plants but not for the tree.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה, talking about rain.

phrases.english: It makes sense: for plants and not for the tree,
you can find it where gentle rain came,
and heavy rain did not come.
For the tree and not for plants,
where heavy rain came, and gentle rain did not come.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָרְדוּ לַצְּמָחִין אֲבָל לֹא לָאִילָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the משנה's cases of partial rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Gentle rain alone helps plants, and heavy rain alone helps trees.

steps.title: How rain can help both plants and trees but not fill the cisterns
steps.stepSummary: Both kinds of rain fell, so plants and trees were helped, but not enough fell to fill the בורות, שיחין and מערות.
steps.simpleTranslation: For both this and that, but not for cisterns, ditches and caves: you can find it where heavy and gentle rain both came, but not a lot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the משנה's third case, still under "it makes sense," and keeps building toward the harder question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the type of rain was right but the amount was too small. Plants and trees were helped, but there was not enough extra water to fill the storage pits for the summer.

keyTerms.meaning: Ditches and caves that hold water

phrases.english: For this and that, but not for the cisterns
phrases.notes: "This and that" means plants and trees.

phrases.english: and not for the ditches and caves,
you can find it where heavy and gentle rain came,
but a lot did not come.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָזֶה וְלָזֶה אֲבָל לֹא לַבּוֹרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of cases that make sense.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both kinds of rain fell, but in too small an amount to fill the storage pits.

steps.title: How can rain fill the cisterns but help neither plants nor trees?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with the opposite case, rain that fills the בורות but helps neither plants nor trees, and asks how that could happen.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about what was taught in a ברייתא: rain fell enough for cisterns, ditches and caves, but not for this or that. How can you find that?
steps.whatsHappening: Now comes the hard question that the word בשלמא was setting up. The גמרא asks how so much water could fall without helping any plants or trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If enough rain fell to fill the pits, you would expect the plants and trees to be helped too. So the case in the ברייתא sounds impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: But what about what was taught in a ברייתא?
How can you find this case?

phrases.english: But that which was taught in a ברייתא:
They fell for cisterns, for ditches and for caves
but not for this and that,
how can you find it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with the cases that made sense in steps 5 and 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How could rain fill the storage pits but help no plants or trees?

steps.title: The answer: a single heavy downpour
steps.stepSummary: The answer is a sudden pouring rain. It fills the pits but runs off without soaking the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where it came as a pouring downpour.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the rain came all at once in a pour, so it filled the בורות but did not help the plants or trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pouring rain runs off fast and collects in pits instead of soaking into the soil. So a lot of water can fall and still not help anything that grows.
steps.whatToRemember: How much rain falls is not the only thing that matters. Gentle rain helps plants, heavy rain helps trees, a lot of rain fills the pits, and a single downpour fills the pits but helps nothing that grows.

phrases.english: Where it came in a downpour.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲתָיא בִּשְׁפִיכוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A sudden downpour fills the pits but runs off without helping plants or trees.

steps.title: Deadlines for sounding the alarm over trees and water pits
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that the alarm is sounded for trees near פסח and for water pits near סוכות, but right away if there is no drinking water.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: they sound the alarm over trees near פסח, and over cisterns, ditches and caves near סוכות. If people have no water to drink, they sound the alarm right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that tells us the deadline for sounding the alarm over each kind of rain shortage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the earlier steps that separated rain for trees from rain that fills pits. Trees need their rain by פסח, so that is their deadline. Water pits can wait until סוכות, unless there is nothing left to drink, which is an emergency that cannot wait.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught; introduces a ברייתא
They sound the alarm, meaning they declare a public crisis with fasting and prayer
The Festival; here it means סוכות

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that each kind of rain shortage has its own timetable, and that a danger to drinking water overrides every timetable.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
They sound the alarm over trees
near פסח;
over cisterns, ditches and caves
near the Festival.
phrases.notes: When the גמרא just says 'the חג' with no name, it means סוכות.

phrases.english: And if they have no water to drink,
they sound the alarm over them immediately.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַתְרִיעִין עַל הָאִילָנוֹת בִּפְרוֹס הַפֶּסַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the split between tree rain and pit rain from steps 5-8 to set separate deadlines for the alarm.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trees: alarm near פסח. Water pits: alarm near סוכות. No drinking water: alarm right away.

steps.title: What 'immediately' means
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains that 'immediately' means the usual series of fast days: Monday, Thursday and Monday.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is their 'immediately'? Monday, Thursday and Monday.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא pauses to define its own word 'immediately' (מיד).
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Immediately' does not mean that very day. It means they do not wait for the festival deadline and go straight to the regular fast schedule of Monday, Thursday and Monday.

keyTerms.meaning: Which is it? What is meant by it?
Monday, Thursday and Monday, the usual order of public fast days

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'immediately' as 'the same day'. It means the next round of Monday-Thursday-Monday fasts, without waiting for the deadline.

phrases.english: And what is their 'immediately'?
Monday, Thursday and Monday.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵיזֶהוּ מִיָּד שֶׁלָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the word 'immediately' used at the end of step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Immediately' means on the Monday-Thursday-Monday fast schedule.

steps.title: The alarm is only for the affected district
steps.stepSummary: For all these shortages, the alarm is sounded only in the region that is suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for all of them, they sound the alarm only in their own district.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a limit on where the alarm is sounded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A drought may hit one area and not another. Only the area that is actually suffering sounds the alarm. Places where rain is falling normally do not.

keyTerms.meaning: All of them, meaning all the cases just listed

phrases.english: And for all of them
they do not sound the alarm over them
except in their own district.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל כּוּלָּן אֵין מַתְרִיעִין עֲלֵיהֶן אֶלָּא בָּאִפַּרְכִיָּא שֶׁלָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the alarms from step 9 to the area that is affected.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The alarm is sounded only in the district that is affected.

steps.title: Diphtheria: alarm only when it kills
steps.stepSummary: For אסכרא, the alarm is sounded only when people are dying from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: With אסכרא, when it causes death they sound the alarm. When it does not cause death they do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves from rain to disease and gives the rule for אסכרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the illness is deadly. A mild outbreak is not treated as a public crisis. A deadly one is.

phrases.english: And diphtheria:
when it has death in it,
they sound the alarm over it.
When it has no death in it,
they do not sound the alarm over it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַסְכָּרָא, בִּזְמַן שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ מִיתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same ברייתא, now applying the alarm to disease.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Alarm for אסכרא only when it is deadly.

steps.title: Locusts in any amount, and grasshoppers in dispute
steps.stepSummary: The alarm is sounded for even a few locusts. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר adds grasshoppers.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sound the alarm over locusts, even a small number. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: even over grasshoppers.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with locusts and records a disagreement about grasshoppers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With locusts, even a few are enough, so no minimum amount is needed. The first opinion does not include the חגב, a lesser kind of locust. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that the חגב also calls for an alarm.

keyTerms.meaning: Grasshopper, a lesser kind of locust

phrases.english: And they sound the alarm over locusts
in any amount.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Even over grasshoppers.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַתְרִיעִין עַל הַגּוֹבַאי בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same ברייתא, moving from disease to locusts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Locusts: alarm for any amount. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: grasshoppers too.
steps.whatToRemember: First ברייתא: trees by פסח, pits by סוכות, no drinking water means right away (Monday-Thursday-Monday). Only the affected district sounds the alarm. אסכרא only when deadly. Locusts in any amount. Grasshoppers are in dispute.

steps.title: Trees in the other six years, water pits even in שביעית
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא rules that the alarm for trees applies only in the six regular years, but the alarm for water pits applies even in שביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: they sound the alarm over trees in the other years of the seven-year cycle. Over cisterns, ditches and caves, they do so even in the seventh year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that asks whether the alarm still applies in the שמיטה year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water is needed every year, so the alarm for water pits applies even in שביעית. Trees are treated differently. Their alarm is limited to the other six years of the cycle, and the ברייתא does not say why.

keyTerms.meaning: The seventh year of the cycle, the שמיטה year
The years of the seven-year cycle

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
They sound the alarm over trees
in the other years of the seven-year cycle.

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַבּוֹרוֹת וְעַל הַשִּׁיחִין וְעַל הַמְּעָרוֹת
phrases.english: Over cisterns, ditches and caves,
even in the seventh year.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַתְרִיעִין עַל הָאִילָנוֹת בִּשְׁאָר שְׁנֵי שָׁבוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא adds the question of timing within the seven-year cycle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trees: alarm only in the six regular years. Water pits: alarm even in שביעית.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: trees too in שביעית, for the poor
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the alarm is sounded for trees even in שביעית, because the poor depend on them for food.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: even for trees in the seventh year, because they provide food for the poor.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the first opinion in the ברייתא about trees in שביעית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reason is that the fruit of שביעית is a source of food for the poor. If the trees fail, the poor lose that food, so it is a crisis worth the alarm even in the שמיטה year.
steps.whyThisMatters: His reason shows that sounding the alarm is about protecting people's survival, especially the weakest, and not only about the owner's crops.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even over trees in the seventh year,
because they provide sustenance for the poor.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הָאִילָנוֹת בַּשְּׁבִיעִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in step 14 about trees in שביעית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Alarm for trees even in שביעית, because the poor live from them.
steps.whatToRemember: In שביעית, everyone agrees the alarm is sounded for water pits. For trees there is a dispute: the first opinion says no, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says yes, for the sake of the poor.

steps.title: Sounding the alarm for aftergrowths in the seventh year
steps.stepSummary: A different ברייתא (תניא אידך) repeats the same rulings as the one in steps 14 and 15. In its version, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל just says 'even for trees', and it adds that the alarm is sounded for ספיחין in שביעית because they feed the poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: The alarm is sounded for trees in the other years of the seven-year cycle. For cisterns, ditches and caves, it is sounded even in the seventh year. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: even for trees. The alarm is also sounded for aftergrowths in the seventh year, because the poor get their food from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a second, parallel ברייתא. Most of it matches the one in steps 14 and 15, but it adds one more ruling: the alarm is sounded in שביעית for ספיחין, plants that grow back by themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שביעית no one plants. Even so, ספיחין are allowed to be eaten, so the poor live on them. Since real people depend on them for food, a threat to them is a true emergency, even in a year with no farming.

keyTerms.meaning: They sound the alarm (cry out and fast because of a disaster)
The seventh year, when the land rests from farming
Aftergrowths: crops that grow back by themselves without planting

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
They sound the alarm for trees
in the other years of the seven-year cycle.

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַבּוֹרוֹת עַל הַשִּׁיחִין וְעַל הַמְּעָרוֹת
phrases.english: For cisterns, for ditches, and for caves,
even in the seventh year.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even for trees.
They sound the alarm for aftergrowths in the seventh year,
because they provide food for the poor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְרִיעִין עַל הַסְּפִיחִין בַּשְּׁבִיעִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ברייתא to the one in steps 14 and 15. It repeats the same rulings and adds a ruling about ספיחין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The alarm is sounded for ספיחין in שביעית, because the poor depend on them for food.

steps.title: Since the בית המקדש was destroyed, rain has been meager
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא teaches that since the חורבן, rain has been meager, and he lists four kinds of years: heavy rain, light rain, rain on time, and rain not on time.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא said: Since the day the בית המקדש was destroyed, rain has become meager for the world. Some years have a lot of rain and some have little. Some years the rain comes at the right time, and some years it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a new ברייתא. It lists four kinds of rainy years, and the next steps will explain each one with a parable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate questions here: how much rain falls (a lot or a little) and when it falls (on time or late). The list sets up the parables that come next, where each kind of year is compared to a servant getting his food from his master.

keyTerms.meaning: Shriveled or meager; here, rain that is not enough

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא:
phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata said:
From the day the Temple was destroyed,
rain has become meager for the world.
There is a year whose rains are plentiful,
and there is a year whose rains are scarce.
There is a year whose rains fall at their proper time,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ שָׁנָה שֶׁאֵין גְּשָׁמֶיהָ יוֹרְדִין בִּזְמַנָּן.
phrases.english: and there is a year whose rains do not fall at their proper time.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, a teaching about the nature of rain since the חורבן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the חורבן, rain has been meager. Years differ both in how much rain falls and in whether it falls on time.

steps.title: Rain on time is like getting food on Sunday
steps.stepSummary: A year when the rain comes on time is like a servant who gets his weekly food on Sunday. He has time to bake it properly and eat it properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year with rain on time like? It is like a servant whose master gave him his food on Sunday. His dough ends up baked properly and eaten properly.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא explains the first kind of year from his list, rain on time, with a parable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting the week's food at the start of the week means there is plenty of time to prepare it and spread it out over the days. In the same way, rain that comes on time gives the crops what they need when they need it.

keyTerms.meaning: To what can it be compared? (opens a parable)
The first day of the week, Sunday
Properly, the way it should be

phrases.english: A year whose rains fall at their proper time,
what is it like?
Like a servant whose master gave him his food
on Sunday.
The dough ends up baked properly,
and eaten properly.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ יוֹרְדִין בִּזְמַנָּן לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the "rain on time" year from the list in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain on time is like food given at the start of the week: everything gets prepared and used properly.

steps.title: Late rain is like getting food on Friday
steps.stepSummary: A year when the rain does not come on time is like a servant who gets his food on ערב שבת. There is no time to bake it properly or eat it properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year with rain not on time like? It is like a servant whose master gave him his food on ערב שבת. His dough ends up baked improperly and eaten improperly.
steps.whatsHappening: The parable is now reversed to explain the year when the rain comes late.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food handed over just before שבת leaves no time to prepare it well, so it is rushed and wasted. Late rain is the same: the water comes, but too late to help the crops the right way.

keyTerms.meaning: Improperly, not the way it should be

phrases.english: A year whose rains do not fall at their proper time,
what is it like?
Like a servant whose master gave him his food
on Friday, just before Shabbat.
The dough ends up baked improperly,
and eaten improperly.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁאֵין גְּשָׁמֶיהָ יוֹרְדִין בִּזְמַנָּן לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite of step 18: food given late instead of early.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Late rain is like food given at the last minute: it cannot be prepared or used properly.

steps.title: Heavy rain is like getting all the food at once
steps.stepSummary: A year of heavy rain is like a servant who gets all his food at once. The mill loses the same amount whether it grinds a large כור or a small קב, so doing it all at once saves food.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a year with plentiful rain like? It is like a servant whose master gave him all his food at once. The mill loses as much from a כור as it does from a קב, and the dough loses as much from a כור as it does from a קב.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא explains the year of plentiful rain with a parable about grinding and dough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every time you grind or knead, a fixed amount is lost, no matter how big the batch is. If the servant gets everything at once, he grinds one time and loses that amount only once. Plentiful rain coming together is compared to this efficient, one-time processing.

phrases.english: A year whose rains are plentiful,
what is it like?
Like a servant whose master gave him his food
all at once.
The mill ends up using up from a כור
phrases.notes: "Grinding" here means what gets lost in the milling. The mill loses the same amount whether the batch is big or small.

phrases.english: the same amount it uses up from a קב,
and the dough ends up losing from a כור
as much as it loses from a קב.
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected wording that some versions add.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מְרוּבִּין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the timing of rain (steps 18 and 19) to the amount of rain, starting with plentiful years.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Plentiful rain is like receiving everything at once: the fixed loss happens only one time, so less is wasted overall.

steps.title: A year of little rain is like food given bit by bit
steps.stepSummary: A year with little rain is like a servant who gets his food a little at a time, so the same waste happens on every small batch.
steps.simpleTranslation: A year with little rain is like a servant whose master gives him food a little at a time. The mill loses as much from a small קב as it would from a big כור, and the dough loses as much from a קב as from a כור. So he ends up with much less.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר בן פרטא gives the opposite of the last parable. Here the rain comes in small amounts, like a servant fed little by little.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every time grain is ground or dough is made, a fixed amount is lost. If you do it once with a big כור, you lose that amount once. If you do it many times with small קבין, you lose it again and again, so small rains waste more.

phrases.english: A year whose rains are few
what is it like?
Like a servant whose master gave him
his food little by little.
It turns out that the mill,
the amount it would grind away from a כור
phrases.notes: A mill swallows up a fixed bit of flour each time it is used, so many small grindings lose much more in total.

phrases.english: it grinds away from each קב.
It turns out that the dough,
however much is lost from a כור
is lost from each קב.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁנָה שֶׁגְּשָׁמֶיהָ מוּעָטִין לְמָה הוּא דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite case of step 20: food given in small pieces instead of all at once.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A year of meager rain wastes more, like food given in small portions where the loss repeats with each batch.

steps.title: Another parable: plenty of water for kneading clay
steps.stepSummary: A second way to explain why heavy rain is good: like kneading clay, plenty of water does the job well, while too little runs out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: a year of heavy rain is like a person kneading clay. If he has lots of water, it does not run out and the clay is kneaded well. If he has little water, it runs out and the clay is not kneaded well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different parable (דבר אחר) for why a year of plentiful rain is a blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the picture is the ground itself, like clay that needs to be soaked. Lots of rain soaks the earth fully, but a little rain is used up before the soil is properly ready.

phrases.english: Another explanation:
when the year's rains are plentiful,
what is it like?
Like a person kneading clay.
If he has a lot of water,
the water does not run out,
and the clay is kneaded well.
If he has only a little water,
the water runs out,
and the clay is not kneaded well.

steps.whatToRemember: Plentiful rain is a blessing: little rain gets used up and wasted, like small food portions or too little water for clay.
steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second parable for the same idea that heavy rain is better than light rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Plentiful rain properly soaks the land, like enough water kneads clay well.

steps.title: The pilgrims have no water, and נקדימון makes a deal
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא story begins: the pilgrims in ירושלים had no water, so נקדימון בן גוריון borrowed twelve wells from an officer with a deadline to repay.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once all Israel came up to ירושלים for the festival and had no water to drink. נקדימון בן גוריון went to an officer and said: Lend me twelve wells of water for the pilgrims, and I will give you back twelve springs of water. If I don't, I will pay you twelve talents of silver. And the officer set a deadline.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story from a ברייתא about rain coming in a time of need. This step sets up the deal that the rest of the story depends on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נקדימון is betting that rain will fall and refill the officer's wells before the deadline. If it doesn't, he must pay a huge sum of silver, so the tension of the story is set.

keyTerms.meaning: a talent of silver, a very large sum

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Once all of Israel went up
for the festival to Jerusalem,
and they had no water to drink.
Nakdimon ben Guryon went
to a certain officer,
and said to him:
Lend me twelve wells of water
for the pilgrims,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲנִי אֶתֵּן לָךְ שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה עֵינוֹת מַיִם.
phrases.english: and I will give you back twelve springs of water.
And if I do not give them to you,

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵינִי נוֹתֵן לָךְ שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה כִּכַּר כֶּסֶף,
phrases.english: I will give you twelve talents of silver.
And he set him a deadline.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: פַּעַם אַחַת עָלוּ כׇּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לָרֶגֶל לִירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from parables about rain to a story about rain coming miraculously.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story setup: נקדימון borrows water for the pilgrims, promising water back or twelve talents of silver by a deadline.

steps.title: Deadline day: the morning demand
steps.stepSummary: The deadline arrives with no rain; in the morning the officer demands water or money, and נקדימון says the whole day is still his.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the deadline came and no rain had fallen, in the morning the officer sent: Send me the water or the money you owe me. נקדימון answered: I still have time; the whole day is mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to the deadline day. The officer asks for payment, and נקדימון holds him off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נקדימון points out that the deadline lasts until the end of the day, so he is not late yet. He is still hoping for rain.

phrases.english: When the deadline arrived
and no rain had fallen,
in the morning the officer sent to him:

phrases.aramaic: שַׁגֵּר לִי אוֹ מַיִם אוֹ מָעוֹת
phrases.english: Send me either the water or the money
that you owe me.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלַח לוֹ: עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי זְמַן,
phrases.english: He sent back to him: I still have time,
the whole day is mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן וְלֹא יֵרְדוּ גְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: the deadline set in step 23 has arrived.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the morning of the deadline, נקדימון says he has the whole day to pay.

steps.title: Noon and afternoon: the officer keeps asking
steps.stepSummary: The officer demands payment again at noon and again in the afternoon, and each time נקדימון says there is still time left in the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: At noon the officer sent: Send me the water or the money you owe me. He answered: I still have time left in the day. In the afternoon he sent: Send me the water or the money you owe me. He answered: I still have time left in the day.
steps.whatsHappening: The story builds tension as the day goes on with no rain. The officer asks twice more, and נקדימון gives the same answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repeated demand shows the time running out. Still no rain has come, so the reader is waiting to see how נקדימון will be saved.

phrases.english: At noon he sent to him:

phrases.aramaic: שַׁגֵּר לִי אוֹ מַיִם אוֹ מָעוֹת
phrases.english: Send me either the water or the money
that you owe me.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלַח לוֹ: עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי שְׁהוּת בַּיּוֹם.
phrases.english: He sent back to him: I still have time left in the day.
In the afternoon he sent to him:
Send me the water or the money
that you owe me.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלַח לוֹ: עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי שְׁהוּת בַּיּוֹם.
phrases.english: He sent back to him: I still have time left in the day.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּצָּהֳרַיִים שָׁלַח לוֹ: שַׁגֵּר לִי אוֹ מַיִם אוֹ מָעוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בְּיָדְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the morning exchange of step 24 at later times of the day.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: At noon and in the afternoon, נקדימון again says there is still time left.

steps.title: The officer mocks נקדימון
steps.stepSummary: The officer laughs at נקדימון, pointing out that no rain fell all year, and his words continue into the next section.
steps.simpleTranslation: That officer mocked him and said: The whole year no rain has fallen,
steps.whatsHappening: The officer begins to make fun of נקדימון's hope for rain. His sentence is not finished yet; it continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The officer's point is that if it hasn't rained all year, there is no chance of rain in the last few hours. This sets up the miracle that is coming.

phrases.english: That officer mocked him,
saying: The whole year
no rain has fallen,

steps.triggerLanguage: לִגְלֵג עָלָיו אוֹתוֹ הֶגְמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the last of נקדימון's replies, the officer turns to mockery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The officer mocks נקדימון's hope, since no rain fell all year.
